newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says Australia to back WTO entry bid.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says Australia to back WTO entry bid.

text.p: Taiwan has agreed to import 2,000 Australian cars and lower duties on Australian beef to ensure Canberra's support of its entry to the World Trade Organisation, the Central News Agency reported on Friday.

The Board of Foreign Trade said Taipei and Canberra had completed bilateral trade talks on Taiwan's WTO entry, making Australia the 11th WTO member to complete such negotiations with Taiwan, the state-funded agency said.
The sides would sign in the near term a formal agreement with Canberra pledging to support Taiwan's membership bid.
Taiwan wants join the WTO in 1997, but faces U.S. and other Western opposition over trade barriers as well as rival China's determination not to allow the island's entry before its own.
The board officials said Taiwan had made similar compromises on car imports with Malaysia, Mexico and South Africa to win their support for its entry to the world trade body.
The officials said imports of 2,000 Australian cars should have little impact on local production as Australian cars are not very competitive in the market.
Taipei agreed to lower import tariffs on Australian beef by 10 percent in the first half of 1997 and other agricultural and industrial products by around 40 percent.
In September, Canberra's minister for primary industries and energy John Anderson headed a trade delegation of 120 Australian firms to Taiwan despite China's heated protests.
Taiwan now has completed bilateral talks with South Africa, Turkey, Malaysia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, the Philippines, El Salvador, Colombia, Uruguay and Australia.
China, whose entry has been blocked by the United States, Europe, Japan and Canada over market obstacles, has seen Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949.

Beijing insists it should join first, with Taiwan to follow not as a sovereign but as a separate customs territory under a model pioneered by Hong Kong, which will retain a separate trade identity after returning to Chinese rule in mid-1997.
Taiwan has urged the world trade body not to be swayed by China's political agenda when considering its entry.
Taiwan applied in 1990 to join the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, under the name Chinese Taipei. GATT was replaced by the WTO in January 1995.
